title: Given courses with prerequisites, provide a single approach that both detects whether all courses can be finished (Course Schedule I) and, when possible, returns a valid completion order (Course Schedule II), using topological sorting.
shortTitle: Course Schedule I / II unified — detect cycle and produce order

s1_definition.profdef: A single Kahn's-algorithm pass answers both variants: the boolean feasibility is whether every course is emitted, and the order is the emitted sequence itself. Course Schedule I returns the emitted-count-equals-total check, while Course Schedule II returns the emitted order when complete or an empty result on a cycle.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of one routine that both tells you whether a project plan is doable and hands you the actual step order when it is. You process steps as their prerequisites clear, recording the sequence. If every step gets recorded, the plan is doable and the sequence is your schedule; if some steps never clear, the plan has a circular dependency and there is no schedule.
s1_definition.oneliner: One Kahn's pass gives both answers — feasibility is emitted-count equals total, and the order is the emitted sequence, empty if a cycle blocks completion.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A single Kahn's-algorithm pass answers both variants: the boolean feasibility is whether every course is emitted, and the order is the emitted sequence itself. Course Schedule I returns the emitted-count-equals-total check, while Course Schedule II returns the emitted order when complete or an empty result on a cycle.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of one routine that both tells you whether a project plan is doable and hands you the actual step order when it is. You process steps as their prerequisites clear, recording the sequence. If every step gets recorded, the plan is doable and the sequence is your schedule; if some steps never clear, the plan has a circular dependency and there is no schedule.

**One line to remember:** One Kahn's pass gives both answers — feasibility is emitted-count equals total, and the order is the emitted sequence, empty if a cycle blocks completion.

sections.s2_technical:
Build the adjacency list and in-degree array, enqueue zero-in-degree courses, and run Kahn's algorithm emitting each course as its in-degree reaches zero, exactly as in the ordering variant. For example: `order.add(c); for (n : adj.get(c)) if (--inDegree[n] == 0) queue.add(n);`.

For Course Schedule I, the answer is simply whether the emitted count equals the total number of courses, since that is true precisely when the graph is acyclic. For example: `boolean canFinish = order.size() == numCourses;`.

For Course Schedule II, return the emitted order when it is complete, and an empty array when it is short because a cycle left some courses unemitted. For example: `return order.size() == numCourses ? order : emptyOrder;`. The two variants share every line except the final return shape.

The time is linear in courses plus prerequisites, and the space is the adjacency list, in-degree array, queue, and order. A senior nuance is recognizing that the two LeetCode problems are the same algorithm with different return types, so implementing the ordering variant and deriving the boolean from it avoids duplicating logic, and that the emitted-count check is the single source of truth for both cycle detection and order validity.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a regulatory-filing workflow must both confirm that all filings can be completed given their dependencies and produce the actual filing order. The system must answer both from one computation. This is exactly how the unified Course Schedule works.

Problem 2 — Maintaining two separate code paths for feasibility and order would risk drift, so one pass serves both. This is exactly why the ordering variant is implemented and the boolean derived from it.

The mini-project builds a `FilingScheduler` exposing both canComplete and completionOrder over one Kahn's pass, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input has four filings where one and two follow zero, and three follows one and two.

Step 1: The core pass computes in-degrees: zero for filing zero, one for one and two, two for three.

Step 2: Filing zero is emitted first, decrementing one and two to zero, which are emitted next, each decrementing three.

Step 3: Filing three reaches in-degree zero and is emitted last, giving the order zero, one, two, three with size four.

Step 4: canComplete compares the size four to the total four and returns true, answering Course Schedule I.

Step 5: completionOrder sees the full size and returns the emitted order as an array, answering Course Schedule II, both from the same pass.

Step 6: For the cyclic input, the pass emits nothing because neither filing ever reaches in-degree zero, so canComplete returns false and completionOrder returns an empty array.

```text
2026-10-26T23:05:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Regulatory Filing Scheduler (I + II)
2026-10-26T23:05:00Z [INFO] canComplete=true
2026-10-26T23:05:00Z [INFO] Completion order: [0, 1, 2, 3]
2026-10-26T23:05:00Z [INFO] canComplete=false
2026-10-26T23:05:00Z [INFO] Cycle detected; no completion order
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  one Kahn pass → shared result:
    edges 0→1,0→2,1→3,2→3  inDeg 0:0 1:1 2:1 3:2
    emit 0 → 1,2 → 3   order=[0,1,2,3] size=4

  Course Schedule I  : size==n ? → TRUE
  Course Schedule II : size==n ? order : []  → [0,1,2,3]

  cyclic 0↔1 → emit nothing → size 0 → I=FALSE, II=[]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Course Schedule I and Course Schedule II are the same algorithm with different return shapes, and I implement them as a single Kahn's-algorithm pass to avoid duplicating logic. The core pass builds the adjacency list and in-degree array, enqueues the courses with no prerequisites, and emits each course as its in-degree reaches zero, collecting the emitted sequence.

From that one pass both answers fall out. Course Schedule I, the feasibility question, is simply whether the emitted count equals the total number of courses, which is true exactly when the graph is acyclic. Course Schedule II, the ordering question, returns the emitted sequence when it is complete and an empty array when it is short because a cycle left some courses unemitted. The emitted-count check is the single source of truth for both cycle detection and order validity.

The design point interviewers appreciate is recognizing these as one problem and deriving the boolean from the ordering result rather than writing two separate traversals, which keeps the logic DRY and prevents the two code paths from drifting apart. The cost is linear in courses plus prerequisites.

In my project at National Bank of India, a regulatory-filing workflow needed both a confirmation that all filings could be completed given their dependencies and the actual filing order when they could. One Kahn's pass served both: the emitted order was the schedule, and the emitted-count check told me whether the plan was feasible, so a single well-tested routine answered both questions and a dependency cycle produced a clean negative with an empty order rather than a half-built plan.
